title: Technical introduction
text:
Following international protocol we structured our provincial C-Plan around these key questions (SANBI and UNEP-WCMC 2024; Jung et al. 2025):

What biodiversity and where is it?
What is the state of this biodiversity?
Where and how should conservation efforts be prioritized?

These questions form the basis for the structure of this C-Plan. The first key question involves collation and modelling of data in order to obtain the best available spatial representation of biodiversity. The second is largely concerned with the conservation or risk status of biodiversity that will guide the mapping of biodiversity, and the prioritization analyses in point three.

title: Technical introduction
text:
4.1 Ecosystem representation
Incorporating ecosystem types in the SCP process serves to broadly capture the spatial distribution of distinct-biological communities, and thereby the full suite of species—i.e., gamma diversity (Whittaker 1960)—across the region of interest (Mucina 2024). Following the previous terrestrial SCP for KwaZulu-Natal (Escott 2010), a vegetation-type map formed a robust surrogate for ecosystem types. Vegetation types commonly serve as surrogates for ecosystem types because they largely capture differences in biodiversity patterns across the landscape (SANBI and UNEP-WCMC 2024).
For an up-to-date representation of ecosystem extent, the provincial-vegetation map (i.e., coverage) had to be adjusted. The provincial-vegetation coverage serves as a representation of “natural” vegetation communities prior to GC pressures ca. 1750 (Mucina et al. 2018). Therefore, the coverage had to be adjusted to reflect the current state of ecosystems using the best available data.

title: Technical introduction
text:
5.1 Introduction
The broad-ranging approach for representation of biodiversity in the SCP was complemented by a targeted approach (see Section 4.1.2). The targeted approach required a systematic selection of species (SANBI and UNEP-WCMC 2024). Ezemvelo KZN Wildlife scientists and a broad range of stakeholders at an SCP inaugural workshop (Elliot 2023), developed the criteria for the inclusion of species in a workshop session with external stakeholders. For the KwaZulu-Natal SCP, these criteria were applied to each grouping of taxa as shown below.

text:

title: Technical introduction
text:
5.3 Taxon‑specific species selection
Following the criteria in Table 1, species were selected for groupings of taxa: amphibians, aquatic species, birds, invertebrates, mammals, and plants.

5.3.1 Amphibians (championed by A. Armstrong)
All endemic, near-endemic, and threatened (CR, EN, VU) species were included.


5.3.2 Aquatic species (championed by S. Khubheka)


5.3.3 Birds (championed by B. Coverdale)


5.3.4 Invertebrates (championed by A. Armstrong)
All endemic, near-endemic and threatened (CR, EN, VU) taxa are included. Only taxa in the Biodiversity Database are included in the analysis.


5.3.5 Mammals (championed by B. Coverdale)


5.3.6 Plants (championed by C. Carbutt)
The targeted plant species list for the updated KZN SCP revision was developed as follows:

An extract of the plant list used for the previous SCP by Escott (2010) was made.
The extract was evaluated by the plant group (Ezemvelo KZN Wildlife + SANBI) at the C‑Plan workshop at Didima, Jan 2025.
The list was further refined and checked.
Species names were updated for taxonomic changes.
Red List status updated to SANBI RL version 2024.
The list was tabled at the July 2025 C‑Plan Steering Committee meeting.
Approved pending minor revision.
Fully revised in Aug 2025 per Steering Committee directives.
~23 taxa were the focus: extinct or widespread non‑endemic taxa removed; endemic/near‑endemic or declining taxa retained.
Final revised list (Aug 2025) was uploaded to MS Teams as directed.



5.3.7 Reptiles (championed by A. Armstrong)
All endemic, near-endemic and threatened (CR, EN, VU) species are included.

title: Landscape Integrity
text:
flowchart LR

a[("|1. Modification</br>coverage")]
b[("|2. Resistance</br>surface")]
c(["|3. Landscape Integrity /</br>Fragmentation metrics"])
d["|4. Corridor identification"]

a --> c
b --> c
c --> d




Figure 1: Overview of the landscape integrity evaluation to idenifying landscape corridors. 1. A modification coverage is used to identify natural, near-natural, and functional areas. 2. By applying a resistance surface of species movement through the modified landscape, 3. a fragmentation analysis can be performed, to 4. identify corridors for species movement, and areas with good landscape integritiy, i.e., high connectivity, sufficient number and size of habitat patches. R Core Team (2025) packages ‘landscapemetrics’ (Hesselbarth et al. 2019) was used to analyse landscape integrity, and ‘gdistance’ (van Etten 2017) to estimate least-cost paths, and ‘grainscape’ (Chubaty, Galpern, and Doctolero 2025) to evaluate graph connectivity.

title: Technical introduction
text:
3.1 Ecosystem representation
Incorporating ecosystem types in the SCP process serves to broadly capture the spatial distribution of distinct-biological communities, and thereby the full suite of species—i.e., gamma diversity (Whittaker 1960)—across the region of interest (Mucina 2024). Following the previous terrestrial SCP for KwaZulu-Natal (Escott 2010), a vegetation-type map formed a robust surrogate for ecosystem types. Vegetation types commonly serve as surrogates for ecosystem types because they largely capture differences in biodiversity patterns across the landscape (SANBI and UNEP-WCMC 2024).
For an up-to-date representation of ecosystem extent, the provincial-vegetation map (i.e., coverage) had to be adjusted. The provincial-vegetation coverage serves as a representation of “natural” vegetation communities prior to GC pressures ca. 1750 (Mucina et al. 2018). Therefore, the coverage had to be adjusted to reflect the current state of ecosystems using the best available data.

title: Technical introduction
text:
4.1 Introduction
The broad-ranging approach for representation of biodiversity in the SCP was complemented by a targeted approach (see Section 3.1.2). The targeted approach required a systematic selection of species (SANBI and UNEP-WCMC 2024). Ezemvelo KZN Wildlife scientists and a broad range of stakeholders at an SCP inaugural workshop (Elliot 2023), developed the criteria for the inclusion of species in a workshop session with external stakeholders. For the KwaZulu-Natal SCP, these criteria were applied to each grouping of taxa as shown below.

title: Technical introduction
text:
4.2 Criteria for inclusion




Table 1: Criteria for inclusion of species in the targeted approach.



IDCriteriaRules1Endemic to KwaZulu-Natal.Feature must be triggered by ≥1 criterion; criteria equal weighting; may include uncertain data but removed if insufficient; consider age and accuracy of data.2Near Endemic to KwaZulu-Natal (50–99% of taxon distribution falls within KwaZulu-Natal).3Threat status (CR, EN, Rare, VU, NT). Global or Regional. Highest threat status taken.4International obligation.5Umbrella species.6Isolated from core known range with genetic differences.7Edge of range species (may be well protected in KZN but globally/regionally threatened).8Life‑history stage essential for protection of species.9Species conservation plan or biodiversity management plan.10Other (specify).11Resource use threat.12Specific populations (e.g., Tembe elephants, berg eland).

title: Technical introduction
text:
4.3 Taxon‑specific species selection
Following the criteria in Table 1, species were selected for groupings of taxa: amphibians, aquatic species, birds, invertebrates, mammals, and plants.

4.3.1 Amphibians (championed by A. Armstrong)
All endemic, near-endemic, and threatened (CR, EN, VU) species were included.


4.3.2 Aquatic species (championed by S. Khubheka)


4.3.3 Birds (championed by B. Coverdale)


4.3.4 Invertebrates (championed by A. Armstrong)
All endemic, near-endemic and threatened (CR, EN, VU) taxa are included. Only taxa in the Biodiversity Database are included in the analysis.


4.3.5 Mammals (championed by B. Coverdale)


4.3.6 Plants (championed by C. Carbutt)
The targeted plant species list for the updated KZN SCP revision was developed as follows:

An extract of the plant list used for the previous SCP by Escott (2010) was made.
The extract was evaluated by the plant group (Ezemvelo KZN Wildlife + SANBI) at the C‑Plan workshop at Didima, Jan 2025.
The list was further refined and checked.
Species names were updated for taxonomic changes.
Red List status updated to SANBI RL version 2024.
The list was tabled at the July 2025 C‑Plan Steering Committee meeting.
Approved pending minor revision.
Fully revised in Aug 2025 per Steering Committee directives.
~23 taxa were the focus: extinct or widespread non‑endemic taxa removed; endemic/near‑endemic or declining taxa retained.
Final revised list (Aug 2025) was uploaded to MS Teams as directed.



4.3.7 Reptiles (championed by A. Armstrong)
All endemic, near-endemic and threatened (CR, EN, VU) species are included.
